newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan launches 5th annual bid to regain U.N. seat.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan launches 5th annual bid to regain U.N. seat.

text.p: Taiwan, kickstarting its fifth annual bid to rejoin the United Nations, said on Wednesday nine of its 30 diplomatic allies had signed a motion asking the U.N. General Assembly to consider membership for the island.

The Nationalist Republic of China on Taiwan, which lost the sole China seat to arch-rival Beijing in 1971, said the bid for U.N. re-entry was no challenge to communist China and urged Beijing to stop trying to turn the island into a global pariah.
"We absolutely will not challenge the current seat occupied by the Chinese communists, and we will not create permanent separation of China," said Taiwan foreign minister John Chang.
"We urge the Chinese communists to stop their coercive measures, which are against the trend of this era," Chang said at a news conference.
The Nationalist Chinese republic and its army fled into exile on Taiwan in 1949 after losing the mainland to the communists in a civil war.
Beijing, which has regarded Taiwan as a rebel-held province ever since, has blocked moves by Taiwan's allies in each of the past four years to gain entry for the republic.
Despite strong local support for an independent Republic of Taiwan, Taipei officially espouses eventual reunion with the mainland -- though only under multiparty democracy.
Taipei is careful to note that it seeks a U.N. seat only for the Republic of China, which has existed since 1912, not a new Taiwan entity.

Beijing denies the existence of the Republic of China, which therefore is not entitled to international recognition, and maintains that the island must be brought under the communist government's sovereignty, by force if necessary.

On Wednesday Taiwan displayed a letter signed by nine of its 30 diplomatic partners -- mostly small states in Central America and Africa -- that said Taipei's exclusion from the world body was "archaic, unjust and unwarranted".

"We ask that the General Assembly re-examine the inadequacy of Resolution 2758 and rescind it, in order to restore without delay to the 21.5 million people of the Republic of China on Taiwan the lawful right to participate in all activities within the U.N. system," the letter said.
Resolution 2758 was the 1971 U.N. decree that expelled Taipei to make way for Beijing.
Among the signatories were Nicaragua, Gambia, Grenada, the Solomon Islands and Swaziland.

Taipei says that until reunification is possible, it retains the right to conduct foreign affairs and seek recognition for its prosperous economy and vibrant democracy during the current period of separation.
